To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a large-scale CRISPR screen of 2000 genomic loci reveals predictable and accurate DNA repair outcomes, and that these outcomes are highly amenable to correction of disease-associated alleles.

1) a large-scale, unbiased CRISPR– Cas9 screen in five human and one mouse cell lines reveals predictable patterns in the spectrum of DNA repair outcomes at thousands of CRISPR targets; 2) a machine learning model, inDelphi, accurately predicts the spectrum of CRIPSR– Cas9-mediated DNA repair outcomes across a range of target sites; and 3) inDelphi predicts precise-50 editing, which is a CRIPSR–Cas9 editing strategy
a machine-learning algorithm can predict with high accuracy the genotypes of DNA repair outcomes at CRISPR– Cas9-nuclease target sites, enabling correction of pathogenic variants in patient cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing outcomes.
the use of CRISPR-Cas9 technology to predict and correct disease-causing mutations in the human genome.
the use of a machine-learning algorithm for predicting the outcomes of DNA repair by the CRISPR–CAS9 system in human cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have developed a machine-learning algorithm that can be used to predict the spectrum of DNA repair outcomes at genomic target sites in human cells.
the authors show that a machine-learning algorithm can be used to predict the outcomes of Cas9-mediated DNA repair in a wide range of human cell types, with a high degree of accuracy.

the study provides a framework for predicting the spectrum of DNA repair outcomes at a target genomic locus, and that this framework can be used to design CRISPR–CAs9-based therapies that are capable of precise repair of disease-associated mutations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the spectrum of DNA repair outcomes at CRISPR– Cas9 target sites is highly predictable and that this prediction can be used to identify target sites where precise, template-free editing is likely.
the authors use a machine learning approach to predict the spectrum and frequency of Cas9-mediated DNA repair outcomes in human genomic targets.
the authors have developed a method for predicting the outcomes of CRISPR-mediated DNA repair in human cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a substantial proportion of guide RNAs are ‘precise 50’—that is, they produce a single, dominant genotype that accounts for at least half of all major editing outcomes.
precise repair is predictable.
precise, template-free repair is predictable and can be applied to correct disease-causing mutations in humans.
